summary: This document defines a YANG data model to configure and manage devices supporting Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM). The model covers PIM configuration, operational state and event notifications.

eli5.summary: PIM helps send one message to many receivers. This document defines a standard form for setting up PIM and checking on it.

what modules does the pim yang model define
how to configure pim with netconf
subtitle: A set of YANG modules for configuring and monitoring PIM multicast routing on a router through NETCONF or RESTCONF.

tldr.problem: Every vendor configured and monitored Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM) in its own way, which made management tools and mapping between vendors harder.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines five YANG modules (base, RP, PIM-SM, PIM-DM and BIDIR-PIM) that augment the standard routing model, covering configuration, operational state, statistics and notifications, with optional features for capabilities not all devices have.
tldr.outcome: A device can expose PIM in a common structure over NETCONF or RESTCONF, and the RFC maps the older PIM-STD-MIB objects onto the new data nodes.

today: RFC 9128 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2022. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the Model Is For
sections.content:
YANG (RFC 7950) is a data modeling language for the configuration and operational state of devices managed with protocols such as NETCONF (RFC 6241) or RESTCONF (RFC 8040). RFC 9128 uses it to describe devices that run Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM).

The model supports the core PIM protocol and many other features, with the non-core ones defined as optional. It follows the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA, RFC 8342), so operational state sits beside the configuration it belongs to in the same hierarchy.
sections.eli5: Routers from different makers all speak PIM, but they have different settings screens. This gives them one shared screen layout.

sections.title: Scope and Optional Capabilities
sections.content:
The model covers PIM Sparse Mode (RFC 7761, including the Source-Specific subset), Dense Mode (RFC 3973) and Bidirectional PIM (RFC 5015). It also covers two extensions: Bootstrap Routers (RFC 5059) and Anycast-RPs (RFC 4610).

It does not cover other multicast protocols such as IGMP/MLD, MSDP, mVPN or mLDP in-band signaling, and not the configuration needed to generate the Multicast Routing Information Base (MRIB). Those are left to separate documents.

The design goal is that any major existing implementation can be said to support the base model, and that other configurations can be expressed through features plus simple vendor augmentations. Not every device supports every capability, so the modules declare many feature statements, and wide constant ranges (such as timer minima and maxima) are used. Vendors are expected to augment the model with their own restrictions.
sections.eli5: The form has a core part everyone fills in and optional pages for fancy features. If your router does not have a feature, you skip that page.

sections.title: Module Organization
sections.content:
The model is split into separate modules so that a device can express exactly which parts of PIM it supports. Objects relevant to only one situation are collected in a container for it. For example, configuration for PIM-SM that does not matter to an SSM-only implementation lives in an asm container.

  • ietf-pim-base: the framework not specific to any PIM mode, imported by the others. It alone is not enough for any PIM mode to operate.
  • ietf-pim-rp: Rendezvous Point features, shared by PIM-SM and BIDIR-PIM but not by PIM-DM.
  • ietf-pim-sm: Sparse Mode, covering both ASM and SSM.
  • ietf-pim-dm: Dense Mode, with no dependency on the RP module.
  • ietf-pim-bidir: Bidirectional PIM, which augments both the base and RP modules.

The base module augments /rt:routing/rt:control-plane-protocols from the routing model (RFC 8349) rather than the per-protocol-instance node, because PIM is meant to be enabled as a single instance on a network instance or logical network element. The presence of the top-level pim container enables PIM.
sections.eli5: It is like a toolbox with a main drawer and extra trays: one tray for each kind of PIM. You only open the trays you need.

sections.title: Base Module Data: Interfaces and Neighbors
sections.content:
Under pim there is global graceful-restart configuration, a list of address-family entries, and an interfaces list. Per address family, the model offers statistics (counters for errors, queue, received and sent messages by type), and topology-tree-info with IPv4 and IPv6 route entries keyed by group, source address and whether the entry is on the RP tree.

The address family appears both under the PIM instance and under each interface. The RFC explains this makes life easier for implementations that do not support some options per address family; such an implementation can add a deviation, for instance requiring the IPv6 DR priority to match the IPv4 one.

Each interface can configure things like a BFD client, dr-priority, hello-interval, hello hold time or multiplier, join/prune interval and hold time or multiplier, override-interval and propagation-delay, mostly gated behind features. Read-only data includes oper-status, gen-id, the interface addresses and the DR address, plus a read-only list of neighbors with their expiry, DR priority, generation ID, LAN prune delay information and up-time.

The base module also defines two notifications, pim-neighbor-event and pim-interface-event.
sections.eli5: For each network plug on the router, you can set how often it says hello and see who its neighbors are, like a class list with each kid's last check-in.

sections.title: Rendezvous Points, BSRs and Mode Modules
sections.content:
The RP module covers static RPs (lists of IPv4 or IPv6 RP addresses), the bootstrap router (BSR) feature, and read-only state. BSR configuration includes a BSR candidate, with hash mask length and priority, and RP candidates by interface or address. Operational data lists known RPs, with the source of the information, up-time and expiration, and RP-to-group mappings. A pim-rp-event notification reports RP-related events.

The PIM-SM module adds Anycast-RP configuration and SPT-switch settings under asm, an ssm container with a range policy, a per-interface sm container with a passive flag, and optional policy and override settings on static RPs.

The PIM-DM module is minimal: it only adds a dm presence container at the address-family and interface levels. The BIDIR-PIM module adds designated-forwarder election settings (offer-interval, backoff-interval, offer-multiplier), a bidir-capable flag on neighbors, and read-only DF election state per RP and interface.
sections.eli5: Multicast needs a meeting spot called a rendezvous point. This part lets you name the meeting spot by hand or let routers vote on it.

sections.title: Relationship to the PIM MIB
sections.content:
Section 5 maps the tables of the older PIM-STD-MIB (RFC 5060) to YANG nodes. For example, pimInterfaceTable corresponds to pim/interfaces/interface, with the MIB's interface index and IP version represented by the interface name and a sublist keyed by address-family.

Other mappings include pimNeighborTable to the neighbor lists, and pimStarGTable, pimSGTable and pimSGRptTable to the topology-tree-info route entries, distinguished by whether source-address is the wildcard and whether is-rpt is true. pimBidirDFElectionTable maps to the interface DF election data. The RFC also lists the per-object correspondences in tables.
sections.eli5: It is a translation chart between the old way of reading router info and the new one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The modules are meant to be accessed through NETCONF, whose mandatory-to-implement secure transport is SSH, or RESTCONF, which uses HTTPS with TLS. The Network Configuration Access Control Model (NACM, RFC 8341) can restrict users to a subset of operations and content.

Writable nodes under /rt:routing/rt:control-plane-protocols/pim-base:pim are sensitive. The RFC lists the graceful-restart subtrees, the RP, SM, DM and BIDIR subtrees, and the interfaces subtree, noting that changes can interrupt or reroute multicast traffic, cause RP malfunctions, or give PIM insufficient or incorrect information. Unauthorized access can adversely affect multicast routing on the local device and the network.

Readable nodes also matter, since unauthorized reads can disclose PIM operational state on the device.
sections.eli5: Changing router settings can break the network, so only trusted people should be allowed to change or even peek at them.
